why: Russell and Whitehead took up Frege's project of deriving arithmetic from pure logic, and rebuilt it with a hierarchy of types after Russell's paradox broke Frege's system.
Gödel took Principia's kind of formal system as the object to analyse, and turned its own machinery of symbols and rules against the hope that it could prove everything.
Gödel answered Hilbert's programme, which asked for a finitary proof that mathematics is consistent and complete, by showing that no such proof can exist for a system as strong as arithmetic.
Church's proof of an unsolvable problem uses Gödel's technique of encoding formulas as numbers, and his definition of calculable functions is matched against Gödel and Herbrand's recursive functions.
Turing's undecidability proof uses a Gödel-style diagonal argument and the idea of encoding a procedure as data, moving the idea from provability to computation.
The title names the target: Turing shows the Entscheidungsproblem, the search for a mechanical test of logical validity, has no solution.
Two independent definitions of 'effectively calculable', by lambda calculus and by machine, turned out to cover exactly the same functions, which is why the Church–Turing thesis is trusted.
McCulloch and Pitts cite Principia and write neural activity in its logical notation, treating a network's behaviour as propositions that can be derived.
They argue that networks given a tape can compute whatever a Turing machine can, tying neurons to the new definition of computation.
Shannon's thesis explicitly applies Boole's algebra of logic to switching circuits.
Boolean switch algebra became the standard way to design the logic of digital machines, the circuits that EDVAC-style computers are made of.
Shannon moved from the algebra of two-valued switches to the mathematics of two-valued information, carrying the binary view from circuits to messages.
The First Draft explicitly uses the McCulloch–Pitts idealised neuron as its basic switching element, so the design can be reasoned about independently of the hardware.
Keeping instructions in memory as data realises the universal machine's central idea in hardware, though the report does not cite Turing and historians debate the direct influence.
ENIAC had to be rewired to change tasks, which took days; a single memory holding the program removes that bottleneck.
Turing argues that because his universal machine can imitate any other computing machine, a digital computer could in principle imitate a mind.
The Dartmouth proposal turns Turing's question into a research programme, conjecturing that any feature of intelligence can be so precisely described that a machine can simulate it.
The proposal lists neuron nets among its topics and names McCulloch and Pitts among those who had worked on the problem.
Cybernetics, with its focus on feedback and control, was the competing framing of the early 1950s; the new name 'artificial intelligence' marked a different emphasis on symbols and programs.
Chomsky tests Shannon-style Markov models of language and shows finite-state sources cannot generate English, then moves to richer phrase-structure grammars.
Stored-program machines made programming a matter of writing instructions into memory; FORTRAN automated that writing so scientists could use them without machine code.
McCarthy adopts Church's lambda notation to define functions in LISP and builds the language around functions applied to arguments.
LISP's eval, an interpreter for the language written in the language, plays the role of Turing's universal machine: one program that can run any other.
LISP was created to give the AI programme a language for symbolic work: lists, recursion and automatic memory management.
Two answers to what a programming language is for: FORTRAN for fast numeric computation, LISP for symbolic structures and recursion.
Dijkstra's analysis of how an algorithm's cost grows with problem size foreshadows complexity theory, which turns that accounting into a general measure.
Hartmanis and Stearns define computational complexity by counting steps of Turing machines, adding cost to Turing's question of what is computable.
Scheme, a LISP dialect, is the language in which the book teaches programming as the building of abstractions.
Engelbart credits Vannevar Bush's vision of a memex, a desk that stores and links a person's records, as the seed of his framework for augmenting the intellect.
Sketchpad is an early working case of the augmentation idea: a person and a computer thinking together through a shared picture rather than through typed codes.
Smalltalk's overlapping windows and its goal of a personal medium for thought carry Engelbart's aim of augmenting the intellect into personal computing.
Berners-Lee's proposal for linked, shared information continues the hypertext thread running from Bush and Engelbart toward networked collaboration.
Hoare published Quicksort as an ALGOL 60 procedure; the language's support for recursion is what makes the algorithm short to state.
Knuth's series gathers sorting methods like Quicksort and analyses their average and worst cases, in the style of analysis the series made standard.
Smalltalk's objects and direct manipulation echo Sketchpad's master and instance drawings and its interactive pictures; Alan Kay has credited Sketchpad as an inspiration.
Shannon's view of signals in terms of frequencies and samples makes spectra worth computing; the FFT makes computing them cheap enough for everyday signal processing and communications.
Later volumes of Knuth's series treat the FFT as standard material when analysing fast arithmetic and polynomial algorithms.
Moore's forecast is about integrated circuits, the packing of transistors onto a single chip, and asks how fast that packing will improve.
Hennessy and Patterson's quantitative design method takes technology trends, such as the steady growth in transistors per chip, as the baseline for architecture.
Cook's NP-completeness works inside the framework of time-bounded Turing machine computation that Hartmanis and Stearns set up, asking which problems can be solved in polynomial time.
Amdahl analyses the limits of speeding up the sequential stored-program machine by adding processors.
Hennessy and Patterson make Amdahl's law the standard statement of the principle that speedup is limited by the part of a task you do not improve.
Structured control flow answers the tangled branching that early languages such as FORTRAN encouraged.
ALGOL 60's blocks, conditionals and loops show the structured alternative Dijkstra argues programs should be built from.
Dijkstra's case for disciplined program structure was part of the debate at the NATO conference that named the software crisis.
The THE system applies the same discipline of structure to a whole operating system, built in layers that can each be understood and tested on their own.
Hoare's axioms cover the structured constructs Dijkstra argued for, sequence, choice and loop, whose pieces can be reasoned about one at a time.
Hoare's proofs about programs use the deductive style of formal logic: axioms and rules of inference from which properties are derived step by step.
Hoare builds his axioms for the kind of structured, ALGOL-like language the ALGOL 60 report had defined.
Model checking removes the burden of hand-written Hoare-style proofs by checking finite-state systems automatically.
Liskov and Wing specify the behaviour of subtypes with preconditions and postconditions, the vocabulary Hoare's triples introduced.
Parnas's criteria for splitting systems into modules respond to the software crisis the NATO conference described and to proposals there such as reusable components.
Brooks, writing from his experience of the IBM OS/360 project, takes up the conference's diagnosis that large software projects are late and unreliable and asks why.
UNIX's processes and its small, layered design echo the THE system's idea of building an operating system as a hierarchy of simple parts.
Lamport's logical clocks address coordination of independent processes, the problem Dijkstra's semaphores solved inside one machine, now across machines.
Codd's model answers the dependence problems of the tree and network systems of the day, where programs followed stored pointers and broke when the storage layout changed.
Separating what a query asks from how data is stored made access structures such as indexes a design problem of their own, and B-trees became the standard answer.
Chen sets his model beside Codd's relational model and shows it covers it, offering entities and relationships as the higher-level view from which tables are derived.
System R was built to show that Codd's relational model could be made fast, with the optimizer choosing how to answer queries that state only what is wanted.
Karp starts from Cook's result that satisfiability is NP-complete and shows, by chains of polynomial-time reductions, that twenty more well-known problems are just as hard.
Diffie and Hellman draw on complexity theory for the idea of a function that is easy to compute but hard to invert, the property public-key schemes need.
THE showed that a system can be understood part by part; Parnas asks what each part should hide, so that a change to one decision stays inside one module.
Liskov and Wing's behavioural subtyping builds on abstract data types, where a module's interface, not its internals, is what other code may rely on.
Design patterns advise programming to interfaces and hiding implementation choices, Parnas's principle applied to object-oriented design.
System R's access path selection chooses among scans and B-tree indexes, so its optimizer depends on indexes of the kind Bayer and McCreight introduced.
Cerf and Kahn start from the ARPANET's experience with packet switching and design a protocol that joins it, and other networks, into one internetwork.
The end-to-end arguments generalise a choice at the heart of TCP: keep the network simple and put reliability in the hosts at the ends.
The Web is an application built on the internetwork TCP/IP created, using it to carry linked documents between machines anywhere.
Ritchie and Thompson built UNIX after Bell Labs left Multics, carrying over its hierarchical file system and its command interpreter as an ordinary program, in a far smaller system.
C was designed to write UNIX, and the book presents it as the language of that system.
The principles come from the authors' experience designing Multics, whose protection mechanisms the paper uses as its main examples.
Simula 67's classes and objects were the starting point for Smalltalk's idea of computation as objects, which Kay then simplified into message passing.
Kay has said LISP's simplicity and its idea of a language defined in itself shaped Smalltalk's design.
Design Patterns draws its examples largely from Smalltalk and C++, and several patterns, such as Model-View-Controller, come from the Smalltalk community.
RSA supplied what Diffie and Hellman had only proposed: a concrete trapdoor function that makes public-key encryption and digital signatures work.
Shannon's information-theoretic view of secrecy sets the standard of perfect security; Diffie and Hellman move to a computational standard that needs no pre-shared key.
Bitcoin relies on digital signatures, made possible by public-key cryptography, to prove who may spend a coin.
Newell and Simon's lecture states and defends the research programme the Dartmouth proposal launched: that intelligence is the manipulation of symbols.
List processing, the style of programming that LISP and Newell and Simon's IPL embody, is the practical form of the symbol-system hypothesis.
Connectionism offered a rival picture of intelligence as patterns learned in connection weights, rather than explicit symbols and search.
Brooks's later essay returns to why software remains hard, separating essential difficulties from accidental ones.
The Byzantine generals paper extends the study of ordering events across machines to the harder case where some of the machines are faulty or lying.
Paxos uses the state-machine idea from Lamport's clocks paper: replicas that apply the same commands in the same order stay identical.
Spanner uses tightly synchronised clocks to order transactions worldwide, the physical-time answer to the ordering problem Lamport solved with logical clocks.
Shared-nothing parallel databases keep declarative queries and cost-based optimisation and spread the work across many machines.
C's block structure and structured control flow descend from ALGOL through BCPL and B.
Clarke and Emerson build on Pnueli's use of temporal logic to state properties of concurrent programs, adding a branching-time variant that can be checked automatically.
Paxos solves the agreement problem when machines may crash but not lie, the easier relative of the Byzantine generals' problem.
Bitcoin's proof of work is a way to agree on a ledger when some participants may be dishonest, the open-network cousin of the Byzantine generals' problem.
The Web adds nothing to the network itself: its features live in servers and browsers at the ends, as the end-to-end arguments advise.
SICP builds its model of computation, from procedures as values to the metacircular evaluator, on the ideas of lambda calculus.
The book's abstraction barriers teach information hiding as a way of building programs in layers.
Backpropagation trains networks with hidden layers, overcoming the limits of single-layer perceptrons that Minsky and Papert had stressed.
Backpropagation trains networks of the simple threshold-like units that McCulloch and Pitts introduced as models of neurons.
AlexNet is a deep convolutional network trained by backpropagation, now with graphics processors and a huge labelled dataset.
MapReduce and Google's storage systems run on clusters of commodity machines that share nothing, the architecture Stonebraker argued for.
Liskov and Wing's question, when may one object stand in for another, arises from the inheritance and subclassing of object-oriented languages such as Smalltalk.
Design patterns attack the essential complexity of design by reusing proven designs, one of the promising attacks Brooks named.
Agile methods adopt the incremental growing of software, close contact with users and emphasis on people that Brooks recommended.
PageRank treats the web's links as votes, turning the structure of hypertext into a measure of a page's importance.
Linked, shared information was the memex dream; the Web is its networked, public realisation.
The book borrows the idea of a pattern language from Christopher Alexander's architecture, crediting him for the form of a pattern: a problem, a context and a proven solution.
Hennessy and Patterson measure designs of the stored-program architecture quantitatively, asking which trade-offs pay off on real programs.
Support-vector networks are linear classifiers like the perceptron, made far more powerful by the maximum-margin principle and the kernel trick.
For a decade support-vector machines were the leading rival to multilayer neural networks, with strong guarantees and little tuning.
The book builds reinforcement learning on Bellman's dynamic programming, which supplies its equations for the value of a state.
Turing's child machine, taught by reward and punishment, anticipates the learn-from-feedback idea at the heart of reinforcement learning.
Google's crawling and indexing workloads, which link-based search required, shaped the design of its file system.
Raft was designed explicitly as a consensus algorithm easier to understand than Paxos, which its authors found hard to teach and to build systems on.
Spanner uses Paxos to replicate each piece of its data across machines and datacenters.
XP's small releases and constant feedback put into practice Brooks's advice to grow software incrementally rather than build it all at once.
The Agile Manifesto came from a meeting of the creators of lightweight methods, and XP's values of communication, feedback and responding to change run through it.
The CAP proof works in the asynchronous message-passing model that Lamport's work helped define, where delays make a single global order of events unobtainable.
Dynamo chooses availability over consistency, the trade-off CAP says a partitioned system cannot avoid.
GFS runs on a cluster of cheap machines that each own their disks, the shared-nothing architecture applied to storage.
MapReduce reads its input from, and writes its output to, the Google File System.
Bigtable stores its data and logs in the Google File System.
The paper says its map and reduce operations were inspired by the primitives of the same names in LISP and other functional languages.
Spanner stores data in tablets with a design similar to Bigtable's, adding a time-versioned, transactional layer on top.
Dynamo gives up the relational model's rich queries and strict consistency for a simple key-value store that is always available.
Dynamo offers availability with eventual consistency; Spanner offers strong consistency across the globe, two answers to the same scaling problem.
The Bitcoin paper builds on hash-based proof of work, as in Hashcash, and on timestamp chains secured with Merkle trees.
Differential privacy puts a precise bound on how much an answer can reveal about one person, a definition in the formal, information-theoretic style Shannon began.
MapReduce was built partly to compute Google's search index and other large computations over crawled web pages.
Dynamo uses vector clocks, a refinement of Lamport's logical clocks, to track versions of an item across replicas.
AlexNet is a convolutional network in the line LeCun's group built for handwritten digits, scaled up with GPUs, more data and new training tricks.
On ImageNet, features learned by a deep network beat the support-vector machines on hand-designed features that had topped earlier contests.
ResNet's shortcut connections fix the problem that made very deep networks harder to train than shallower ones, the obstacle that AlexNet-style networks had run into.
Both networks in a GAN are trained by backpropagation, the method that made multilayer networks learnable.
Spanner brings the relational model's schemas and SQL queries back to a database that spans the globe.
The Transformer wraps each of its sublayers in a residual connection, the technique introduced for very deep image networks.
The Transformer removes the step-by-step recurrence of LSTM networks, which limited parallel training and made long-range dependencies hard to learn.
The Transformer builds directly on the attention mechanism introduced for sequence-to-sequence translation, and makes attention the whole model.
BERT is built from the Transformer's encoder, trained to predict masked words using context from both sides.
GPT-3 is a Transformer decoder scaled to 175 billion parameters and trained to predict the next word.
GPT-3 aims to avoid the task-specific fine-tuning data that BERT-style pretrained models still need, by learning tasks from a few examples in the prompt.
Codex is a GPT language model fine-tuned on code, applying the same approach to programming.
SWE-bench was built because benchmarks of the kind Codex introduced, small self-contained functions, no longer tested what models could do on real repositories.
SWE-bench tests models on the tangled, changing real-world work of maintaining software, the kind of essential complexity Brooks said no single tool removes.
Borgmaster keeps its state in a Paxos-based replicated store, so the cluster manager survives machine failures.
Borg runs MapReduce batch jobs alongside user-facing services on the same machines, which is what made sharing a cluster worthwhile.
The SRE book describes running Google's services on Borg, whose automation of scheduling, restarts and placement makes operating at that scale possible.
SRE carries the agile emphasis on feedback, small changes and automation into the running of live services.
Raft is a replicated state machine, the idea from Lamport's clocks paper that replicas applying the same commands in the same order stay identical.
